parole.testo: Borrowed from South Slavic, compare Macedonian јагличе (jagliče), Bulgarian агли́ка (aglíka), Old Church Slavonic ꙗгльць (jaglĭcĭ), Serbo-Croatian jàglac /ја̀глац, Slovene jeglič, Romanian aglică.
Borrowed from South Slavic, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *aviti (“to show, (reflexive) to show oneself, appear”), whence Old Church Slavonic авити (aviti), Serbo-Croatian jáviti /ја́вити.

#Borrowed from South Slavic *bat'a rather than cognate with it. #From Proto-Albanian *batja. According to Orel bac/bacë could be related to Proto-Slavic *bat'a (“elder brother, uncle”) and Proto-Slavic *batja (“id”). Source of Romanian baci (“chief shepherd, cheese-maker”) and Megleno-Romanian/Aroma

parole.significato: same, selfsame, identical, double, twofold, duplex, dual, twin (associated with sub-/objects that were born/created at…
parole.testo: Possibly borrowed from South Slavic, compare Bulgarian близна́к (bliznák, “twin”). Compare also Aromanian biznat (“twin”). Less likely from Latin bigno- (“twin”) suffixed with -ák.
Borrowed from a South Slavic term derived from the otherwise unattested Proto-Slavic *bolьba, a derivative of *bolь (“pain”).

parole.significato: coast, shore, bank (of a river, lake, see)
parole.testo: Borrowed from South Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *bergъ (“bank, shore”). Compare Macedonian брег (breg), Serbo-Croatian brȇg /бре̑г.

Borrowed from South Slavic language, compare Old Church Slavonic болꙗринъ (boljarinŭ, “boyar”), Serbo-Croatian boljar (“boyar”) and Bulgarian боляр (boljar, “boyar”). Ultimately from Bulgar. The adjective, a derivate of buj, was likely influenced by the Slavic word.
Borrowed from South Slavic.

parole.significato: son of a vampire, half-vampire (usually from a vampire father and a human mother)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a South Slavic language, probably Serbo-Croatian vàmpīr / ва̀мпӣр or Bulgarian вампи́р (vampír), ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic *ǫpyrь (“vampire”). Anlaut v- > dh- is recorded in Gheg Albanian, reinforced by folk reanalysis as dham (“tooth”, standard dhëmb) + pi (“drink”).
Borrowed from South Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *glogъ.

Borrowed from South Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *kožuxъ. Compare Macedonian кожув (kožuv) and dialectal Bulgarian кожу́ф (kožúf) for the final -f, regional Serbo-Croatian kòžūn /ко̀жӯн for the final -n and Ottoman Turkish غوجوق (gocuk) and dialectal Greek γκοζιόκας (gkoziókas) for the initial g-. The
Borrowed from South Slavic, compare Bulgarian гради́на (gradína), Serbo-Croatian gràdina /гра̀дина, Romanian grădină.

Borrowed from a South Slavic language, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *gъrstь; compare Old Church Slavonic гръсть (grŭstĭ, “fist, handful”), Serbo-Croatian grst (“handful”), Bulgarian гръст (grăst). An old borrowing, considering the rendering of *-s- as -sh- and *-ъ- as -u-.
Borrowed from South Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *guna. Mediation via Greek γούνα (goúna) or Late Latin gunna has also been suggested.

According to Orel, borrowed from a South Slavic language and ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic *xabiti (“to spoil, to waste”). Compare Old Church Slavonic хабити (xabiti), Serbo-Croatian habiti (“damage, destroy”), and Bulgarian хабя (habja, “destroy, spend; blunt”).
Borrowed from South Slavic, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *kaliti (“to temper”). Compare Serbo-Croatian kaliti.
Borrowed from South Slavic, suffixed with -ër. Compare Serbo-Croatian кита.
From South Slavic; cf. Macedonian коска (koska), Serbo-Croatian kȍska.

parole.significato: die used in a children's dice game
parole.testo: From South Slavic; cf. Macedonian коцка (kocka), Serbo-Croatian kȍcka ‘die, cube’.
From a South Slavic language, in urn from Proto-Slavic *kokošь. Compare Serbo-Croatian kokoš, Bulgarian кокош (kokoš).
Borrowed from South Slavic, compare Bulgarian глогина (glogina), Macedonian глогинка (gloginka), Serbo-Croatian glòginje /гло̀гиње, contaminated by kollo- and Gjon (“John”).
From South Slavic. Compare Bulgarian кош (koš) and Serbo-Croatian kȍš /кош.
Borrowed from a South Slavic language, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *kury (“whore”). Compare Serbo-Croatian курва (“prostitute, slut”), Bulgarian курва (kurva), and Romanian curvă.

Orel suggests from South Slavic, compare Serbo-Croatian lȉh (“exclusive”), lȋh (“false, odd”), Slovene lȋh (“uneven, odd”). However, generally thought to be from Ancient Greek εὐλογία (eulogía) "blessing", with a euphemistic sense development. Compare e.g. the euphemistic synonym "e lume" (the happy
Borrowed from a South Slavic language; compare Serbo-Croatian lòpata (“shovel”), Bulgarian лопата (lopata, “shovel”). Ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic *lopata (“shovel, spade”).
Borrowed from South Slavic, compare dialectal Bulgarian лича́ (ličá, “to announce”).
Borrowed from South Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *mamiti (“to lure, entice”).

*Results from the recombination of mbrazëm, from an earlier *brazën, itself borrowed from South Slavic *porzdьnъ. Compare Bulgarian пра́зен (prázen), Serbo-Croatian prázan /пра́зан. *Directly borrowed from Serbo-Croatian prázan /пра́зан. See also zbraz.
Borrowed from South Slavic , from Proto-Slavic *mečьka (“she-bear”).
From South Slavic; compare Macedonian мол (mol), Serbo-Croatian molj.
Borrowed from South Slavic, compare Serbo-Croatian mrȅža /мре̏жа, Bulgarian мре́жа (mréža), Macedonian мрежа (mreža), Romanian mreajă, Aromanian mreajã.
Borrowed from South Slavic.
Borrowed from South Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *nevoľa. For sense 4 compare Greek ανάγκη (anágki) and Italian bisogno.
Borrowed from South Slavic, compare Serbo-Croatian pȉčka /пи̏чка and Macedonian пи́чка (píčka, “cunt, pussy”).

parole.significato: item of household goods and furniture
parole.testo: Borrowed from South Slavic, compare Bulgarian пля́чка (pljáčka), Serbo-Croatian pljȁčka /пља̏чка.

From a South Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *plugъ (“plough”), itself of Germanic origin, derived from Proto-West Germanic *plōg (“plough”). Compare Serbo-Croatian плуг, Bulgarian плуг (plug), and English plough. Replaced parmendë in most dialects, which came to mean “wooden plough”.
Borrowed from South Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *pokrovъ, whence Serbo-Croatian pòkrov /по̀кров.
Borrowed from South Slavic. Compare Bulgarian поп (pop), Serbo-Croatian поп /pȍp.

parole.significato: to request something to be done, bought, or sent
parole.testo: An early loanword from a South Slavic language, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *porǫčiti (“to hand to, to leave to somebody”), a formation from *rǫka (“hand”). Compare Serbo-Croatian poručiti (“to send word, to inform”).
Borrowed from South Slavic, from Ancient Greek ποτήριον (potḗrion). Compare Romanian potir.
Borrowed from South Slavic, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *podъkova. Compare Bulgarian подко́ва (podkóva), Serbo-Croatian pòtkova /по̀ткова, Romanian potcoavă.
Derivative of prij + -e, probably a calque from South Slavic *vada.
Borrowed from South Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *pobratimъ.
Metathesis of dialectal prutekë, from South Slavic; cf. Bulgarian прътак (prătak), прътец (prătec), Serbo-Croatian prutak, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *prǫtъ.
Borrowed from South Slavic, compare Serbo-Croatian pȑč /пр̏ч, Bulgarian пръч (prăč).
Derived from South Slavic.
From a South Slavic language; compare Serbo-Croatian rob, Macedonian роб (rob), Bulgarian роб (rob), ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic *orbъ (“servant, slave”).
Borrowed from South Slavic. Compare Bulgarian се сели (se seli, “settle down”).
From South Slavic, compare Serbo-Croatian štȓk, Macedonian штрк (štrk), Bulgarian щъ́ркел (štắrkel).
Borrowed from South Slavic, compare Serbo-Croatian sȉsa /си̏са. Compare also Italian sisa.

From a South Slavic language; compare Serbo-Croatian suditi (“to judge, to trial”), Old Church Slavonic сѫдити (sǫditi, “to judge”); ultimately from Proto-Slavic *sǫditi (“to judge”). Borrowed later than the doublet sundoj.

parole.significato: place with huts and pens for shepherds and cattle; shed, fold, barn; hut, shelter
parole.testo: Borrowed from South Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *stanъ (“camp”).
Borrowed from South Slavic, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *strěxa.
Borrowed from South Slavic, compare Serbo-Croatian strȗg /стру̑г (“river branch”), Macedonian струга (struga, “furrow; riverbed”).

parole.significato: incense (resin that emits pungent smoke when burned and is used in religious ceremonies)
parole.testo: From a South Slavic language; compare Bulgarian тамя́н (tamján) and Serbo-Croatian tàmjan. Ultimately from Greek θυμίαμα (thymíama).
Borrowed from South Slavic. Compare Bulgarian троха́ (trohá), Serbo-Croatian trȍha /тро̏ха.

parole.significato: group of villagers helping another fellow villager with agricultural work
parole.testo: Likely from South Slavic, compare Bulgarian опра́ се (oprá se, “to rely on, hope for”), Serbo-Croatian ùprēti se /у̀пре̄ти се, ùprijēti se /у̀прије̄ти се (“to make great effort”). Discarded theories Jokl (1942) derived it from vepër (“work”). Orel (1998) tentatively compared it to Avestan 𐬎𐬞𐬀𐬭𐬋 (upa
Borrowed from South Slavic; compare Serbo-Croatian vedro, vjedro, Bulgarian ведро́ (vedró).
Borrowed from South Slavic.
Borrowed from South Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *veriga (“chain”).
Borrowed from South Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *vydra. Doublet of lundër.
From a South Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *višьňa. Compare Serbo-Croatian ви̏шња, Romanian vișină, Turkish vişne.
Possibly ultimately from South Slavic, compare Bulgarian вискам (viskam, “to whine”), dialectal виск (visk, “shriek”). Alternatively from Visk, hypocoristic of Vinçenc (“Vincent”).
Borrowed from South Slavic, whence Bulgarian влах (vlah) and Serbo-Croatian Vlȁh /Вла̏х, from Proto-Slavic *volxъ (“Roman; Vlach”).
Borrowed from South Slavic, whence Bulgarian вози (vozi), Serbo-Croatian во̀зити /vòziti.
Borrowed from South Slavic.

Borrowed from a South Slavic language, compare Old Church Slavonic законъ (zakonŭ, “law”), Bulgarian закон (zakon, “law, statute”), and Serbo-Croatian zákon (“law, rule”). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *zakonъ (“law”).

Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish گزمك (gezmek, “to walk about, to rove, stroll, wander”). Alternatively, Orel proposes an early borrowing from South Slavic, whence Bulgarian яздьа (jazdʹa) and Serbo-Croatian jezditi.

From Proto-Albanian *krau, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱreh₂u, *ḱrh₂eu (“limb”). Close to Latin crūs. Alternatively from archaic krahi, definite krai (Buzuku), from South Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *krajь (“end; rim, edge; region”) (compare Serbo-Croatian krȃj, Bulgarian край (kraj)). Similar sense dev

Akin to lag (“to wet, moisten”), lëgatë (“marsh”) and possibly laç (“wetland”). Likely a formation from Proto-Indo-European *welg- (“wet, damp”), akin to Proto-Slavic *vòlga (“moisture”). Alternatively borrowed from South Slavic descendants of it, compare Serbo-Croatian vlȁga /вла̏га, Aromanian vlag

Borrowed from a South Slavic language, ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic *lędina (“untilled land”); compare Serbo-Croatian lèdina, Bulgarian леди́на (ledína). Alternatively connected to lëndë, although seemingly unlikely, or perhaps directly from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ-.

Borrowed from South Slavic, ultimately either from Proto-Slavic *pàdati (“fall”) whence Serbo-Croatian nà-padati /на̀-падати (“to attack”) or from Proto-Slavic *pǫditi (“to chase”) whence Macedonian пади (padi, “to chase out”).
Kristoforidhi and Çabej descend it from South Slavic. Alternatively from Turkish vidalı (“threaded, screwed”).
